{{Nihongo|'''Tomoko Ohta'''|太田 朋子|Ōta Tomoko| born Tomoko Harada 原田 朋子<ref name="Jones"/> 7 September 1933, [[Miyoshi, Aichi]]}} is a Japanese scientist and professor emeritus of the [[National Institute of Genetics]]. Ohta works on [[population genetics]]/[[molecular evolution]] and is known for developing the [[nearly neutral theory of evolution]].

Ohta has received many awards, including Japan's [[Order of Culture]] (2016). In 2015, Ohta and [[Richard Lewontin]] were jointly awarded the [[Crafoord Prize]] "for their pioneering analyses and fundamental contributions to the understanding of [[Polymorphism (biology)|genetic polymorphism]]".<ref name="Crafoord">{{cite web |title=The Crafoord Prize in Biosciences 2015 |url=https://www.crafoordprize.se/news/the-crafoord-prize-in-biosciences-2015/ |website=Crafoord Prize |date=14 January 2015 |access-date=28 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="Söderström">{{cite journal |last1=Söderström |first1=Bo |title=Discovery of genetic polymorphism: Richard Lewontin and Tomoko Ohta awarded the Crafoord Prize in Biosciences 2015 |journal=Ambio |date=April 2015 |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=165 |doi=10.1007/s13280-015-0640-1 |pmid=25712534 |pmc=4357622 |bibcode=2015Ambio..44..165S |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s13280-015-0640-1.pdf |access-date=28 February 2023}}</ref>

==Education==
Tomoko Ohta was born near Nagoya<ref name="Sridhar"/> and grew up in Miyoshi-cho in [[Aichi Prefecture]].<ref name="DeBakcsy">{{cite web |last1=DeBakcsy |first1=Dale |title=Breaking Neutral: The Population Genetics of Tomoko Ohta |url=https://womenyoushouldknow.net/population-genetics-tomoko-ohta/ |website=Women You Should Know® |access-date=28 February 2023 |date=27 May 2020}}</ref> She was in the 6th grade in elementary school when [[World War II]] ended.  After the war, there were widespread changes in the social and educational systems, including the introduction of co-education. She attended junior high school in Toyota, and became interested in mathematics and physics. After senior high school, she entered Nagoya University. Having failed the examination for medical school, she transferred to the agriculture department at Tokyo University and majored in horticulture. Ohta graduated from the Agriculture Department of the [[University of Tokyo]] in 1956. After working at a publishing company, she was hired at the [[Kihara Institute for Biological Research]]. There she studied the [[cytogenetics]] of wheat and sugar beets.<ref name="Sridhar">{{cite web |last1=Sridhar |first1=Hari |last2=Ohta |first2=Tomoko |title=Revisiting Ohta 1973 |url=https://reflectionsonpaperspast.wordpress.com/2020/11/22/revisiting-ohta-1973/ |website=Reflections on Papers Past |language=en |date=22 November 2020}}</ref>

Hitoshi Kihara gave Ohta an opportunity to study abroad,<ref name="Ohta R618-R619"/> and in 1962, she entered the graduate program at [[North Carolina State University]] with support from a [[Fulbright scholarship]].<ref name="perspectives"/> Having initially planned to work on plant cytogenetics, she switched her focus to [[population genetics]]. She worked with her advisor, [[Ken-Ichi Kojima]], on problems in stochastic population genetics,<ref name="Ohta R618-R619"/> Ohta completed her PhD in 1966.<ref name="Ohta R618-R619"/>

==Career==
Returning to Japan in 1967, Ohta obtained a post-doctoral position at Japan's [[National Institute of Genetics]] (NIG) under [[Motoo Kimura]], then the only theoretical population geneticist in Japan.<ref name="Ohta R618-R619">{{Citation| last = Ohta| first = Tomoko| title = Tomoko Ohta| journal = Current Biology| volume = 22| issue = 16| pages = R618–R619| doi = 10.1016/j.cub.2012.06.031| pmid = 23082325| year = 2012| doi-access = free | bibcode = 2012CBio...22.R618O|url=https://www.cell.com/current-biology/pdf/S0960-9822(12)00707-5.pdf}}</ref>
Ohta was later promoted to a research position at the National Institute of Genetics where she remained from 1969 to 1996.<ref name="NIG"/>
In April 1984, Ohta became a full professor in the Department of Population Genetics at NIG. She became head of the Department of Population Genetics at NIG in 1988, and served as the vice-director of the National Institute of Genetics from 1989 to 1991.<ref name="perspectives">{{cite web |url=http://authors.library.caltech.edu/5456/1/hrst.mit.edu/hrs/evolution/public/profiles/ohta.html |title=Profile of Tomoko Ohta |website=Perspectives on Molecular Evolution }}</ref> Ohta served as vice-president of the [[Society for the Study of Evolution]] in 1994.<ref>{{cite web |title=Officers and Editors |url=http://www.evolutionsociety.org/file.php?file=sitefiles/Handbook%20files/SSE_Past_Officers_1-13-2022.pdf |website=Society for the Study of Evolution Past |access-date=28 February 2023}}</ref>

==Research==
In the early 1960s, genetic theories about [[natural selection theory|natural selection]]<ref name="NIG"/> assumed that inherited mutations were either harmful, and would be removed from the population, or beneficial, and would be transmitted to future individuals in the population. Based on this assumption, all individuals in a population were expected to be highly similar. However, in 1966, [[Richard Lewontin]] and [[John Lee Hubby]] found a much greater than expected amount of genetic variation among the individuals in a population.  Motoo Kimura proposed a possible explanation, the [[neutral theory of evolution]], to model changes in a population over time. According to his theory, some gene variants were neither advantageous nor harmful and were not affected by natural selection.<ref name="Royal">{{cite web |title=The Crafoord Prize in Biosciences 2015 |url=https://www.crafoordprize.se/app/uploads/2015/01/popcrafoorden2015.pdf |website=The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |access-date=28 February 2023}}</ref>

Having worked on the neutral theory of evolution with Kimura, Ohta became convinced that division into good, neutral and harmful mutations was too simplistic a model to fully explain the observed data.<ref name="Royal"/> She theorized that nearly neutral mutations (neither deleterious nor entirely neutral) still played an important role in [[evolution]].<ref name="Ruse">{{cite book |last1=Ruse |first1=Michael |last2=Travis |first2=Joseph |title=Evolution: The First Four Billion Years |date=1 January 2009 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-06221-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UussEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA767 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="NIG">{{cite web |first=Narumi |last=Sato |title=National Institute of Genetics: OHTA, Tomoko - Professor Emeritus |url=https://www.nig.ac.jp/nig/research/interviews/pioneers-in-genetics/tomoko-ohta|publisher=[[National Institute of Genetics]]|access-date=20 April 2016}}</ref> 
She first developed the slightly deleterious model of molecular evolution, and then a more general form, the [[nearly neutral theory of evolution]].<ref name="McCandlish">{{cite journal |last1=McCandlish |first1=David M. |last2=Stoltzfus |first2=Arlin |last3=Dykhuizen |first3= Daniel E. |title=Modeling Evolution Using the Probability of Fixation: History and Implications |journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology |date=2014 |volume=89 |issue=3 |pages=225–252 |doi=10.1086/677571 |jstor=10.1086/677571 |pmid=25195318 |s2cid=19619966 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1086/677571 |access-date=28 February 2023 |issn=0033-5770|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Razeto-Barry">{{cite journal |last1=Razeto-Barry |first1=Pablo |last2=Díaz |first2=Javier |last3=Vásquez |first3=Rodrigo A. |title=The Nearly Neutral and Selection Theories of Molecular Evolution Under the Fisher Geometrical Framework: Substitution Rate, Population Size, and Complexity |journal=Genetics |date=2012 |volume=191 |issue=2 |pages=523–534 |doi=10.1534/genetics.112.138628 |pmid=22426879 |pmc=3374315 |issn=0016-6731}}</ref><ref name="Steen">{{cite journal |last1=Steen |first1=TY |title=The Case of Ohta Tomoko: A Woman Geneticist in the Neutralist-Selectionist Evolution Controversy |journal=[[Historia Scientiarum]] |series=Second Series |date=29 November 2008 |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=172–184 |url=https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1572824502417888128 |language=en}}</ref> Her theory challenged the position of her mentor Kimura, but they were able to debate fiercely and still maintain both their friendship and their independent positions.<ref name="excentric">{{cite journal|author=Steen, TY. | year=1996 | title=Always an excentric?: A Brief Biography of Motoo Kimura | journal=[[Journal of Genetics]] |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=19–25| doi=10.1007/BF02931748 | s2cid=29545568 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02931748|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Ohta's theory of slightly deleterious fixations introduced a new class of origin-fixation models, with the goal of better explaining observed data.<ref name="McCandlish"/> While most of the mutations that affected encoded proteins were harmful, as long as they were not too significant ("nearly neutral"), they could remain in the population. Ohta also examined the role of chance and population size.  She showed that population size is important in determining whether less-than-optimal variants can spread; in a smaller population, chance will have a greater effect on the set of outcomes, and natural selection will function more poorly. (In effect, rolling a small number of genetic dice is less likely to show a representative distribution of results than rolling a large number of dice.)<ref name="Royal"/> As a result, mutations that are slightly deleterious can become more easily fixed in small than in large populations, through [[genetic drift]].<ref name="Nei">{{cite journal |last1=Nei |first1=Masatoshi |last2=Suzuki |first2=Yoshiyuki |last3=Nozawa |first3=Masafumi |title=The Neutral Theory of Molecular Evolution in the Genomic Era |journal=Annual Review of Genomics and Human Genetics |date=22 September 2010 |volume=11 |pages=265–289 |doi=10.1146/annurev-genom-082908-150129 |pmid=20565254 |url=https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-genom-082908-150129 |access-date=28 February 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
In 1974, Kimura and Ohta proposed a set of five general principles that might influence molecular evolution.<ref name="Royal"/>

When Ohta first published her Nearly Neutral theory, she faced difficulty in attracting the scientific research community's attention and acceptance.<ref name="NIG"/> Supporting data in [[protein evolution]] was sequentially collected in the 1990s, with even more evidence supporting her theory made available throughout the 21st century. There is more and more evidence evolving that supports her nearly neutral theory of evolution.<ref name="Chen"/><ref name="Royal"/><ref name="Ohta R618-R619"/>

{{blockquote|"The nearly neutral theory in its initial form may not explain all aspects of polymorphisms but, almost 50 years after it was first proposed by Tomoko Ohta (Ohta 1973), it still constitutes an excellent starting point for further theoretical developments."<ref name="Chen">{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Jun |last2=Glémin |first2=Sylvain |last3=Lascoux |first3=Martin |title=From Drift to Draft: How Much Do Beneficial Mutations Actually Contribute to Predictions of Ohta's Slightly Deleterious Model of Molecular Evolution? |journal=Genetics |date=April 2020 |volume=214 |issue=4 |pages=1005–1018 |doi=10.1534/genetics.119.302869 |pmid=32015019 |pmc=7153929 |issn=1943-2631}}</ref>}}

==Recognition==
Ohta's work in the field of molecular evolution has been recognized internationally.

* 1981 - Inaugural [[Saruhashi Prize]], Society for the Bright Future of Women Scientists<ref name="perspectives"/>
* 1984 - International Honorary Member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web |title=Tomoko Ohta |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/tomoko-ohta |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |access-date=28 February 2023 |language=en}}</ref>
* 1985 - [[Japan Academy Prize (academics)|Japan Academy Prize]] for "Theoretical Studies on Population Genetics at the Molecular Level"<ref>{{cite web |title=The Imperial Prize, Japan Academy Prize, Duke of Edinburgh Prize Recipients 71st - 80th {{!}} The Japan Academy |url=https://www.japan-acad.go.jp/en/activities/jyusho/071to080.html#anker005 |website=japan-acad.go.jp |access-date=28 February 2023}}</ref>
* 1986 - Avon Special Prize for Women, Avon Japan<ref name="Yount"/>
* 1986 - [[Weldon Memorial Prize]], [[University of Oxford]]<ref name="Yount">{{cite book |last1=Yount |first1=Lisa |title=A to Z of Women in Science and Math |date=2007 |publisher=Infobase Publishing |isbn=978-1-4381-0795-0 |pages=232–233 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=428i2UdWRRAC&pg=PA232 |language=en}}</ref>
* 2002 - Foreign Member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in [[evolutionary biology]] and [[genetics]]<ref name="NAS">{{cite web |title=Tomoko Ohta |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/tomoko-ohta-sk1bvq/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=28 February 2023}}</ref>
* 2002 - [[Person of Cultural Merit]], [[Emperor of Japan]]<ref>{{cite news |title=Emperor to present two awards to Tanaka |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/2002/10/31/announcements/emperor-to-present-two-awards-to-tanaka/ |access-date=28 February 2023 |work=The Japan Times |date=31 October 2002}}</ref>
* 2015 - [[Crafoord Prize]] of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] (shared with [[Richard Lewontin]])<ref name="Crafoord"/>
* 2016 - [[Order of Culture]], [[Emperor of Japan]]<ref name="Jones">{{cite news |url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2016/11/09/issues/called-egalitarian-japan-still-honor-bound |title=So-called egalitarian Japan is still honor-bound | first=Colin P.A. |last=Jones |date= 9 November 2016 |work= Special to the Japan Times}}</ref>
* 2018 - [[Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution]] (SMBE) Motoo Kimura Lifetime Contribution Award<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smbe.org/smbe/AWARDS/FacultyAwards/SMBELifetimeContributionAward.aspx|title=SMBE Lifetime Contribution Award |website=Society for Molecular Biology & Evolution}}</ref>
